SK5030 An XML signature checked against the key the document carries

SignedXml.CheckSignature() with no argument verifies the document against the key written inside the document.

CategorySecurity
Default severityerror
ScopeSemantic
Needs a compilationyes
Runs under --load=looseno
Cached per fileyes
Fixno
Language version floor—
Since2.0
SupersedesS6377

Why

An XML signature is supposed to answer “who signed this”, and the parameterless overload answers “is this document internally consistent” instead. It takes its key from the signature's own KeyInfo element — a part of the document — so an attacker rewrites the payload, signs it with a key pair they generated a second ago, writes their public key into KeyInfo, and the check returns true. Every document can vouch for itself, which means the check distinguishes nothing. That is the whole of the SAML and XML-DSig signature-bypass family, and it is dangerous precisely because the call site reads like a real validation: there is a CheckSignature, it returns a bool, and the code branches on it. The fix is to say which key you trust — CheckSignature(publicKey) with a key from configuration, or CheckSignature(certificate, false) with a certificate you resolved and chain-validated yourself. ⚠ There is no fix on the diagnostic because the edit is a decision rather than a substitution: which key is trusted, and where it comes from, is the question the rule exists to make somebody answer.

Example

Instead of:

var signed = new SignedXml(document);
signed.LoadXml(signatureElement);
if (signed.CheckSignature()) {
    Accept(document);
}

Write:

var signed = new SignedXml(document);
signed.LoadXml(signatureElement);
if (signed.CheckSignature(trustedPublicKey)) {
    Accept(document);
}

When it does not fire

One fact decides it and the fact is local: an invocation of CheckSignature with zero arguments whose containing type derives from System.Security.Cryptography.Xml.SignedXml. There is no aliasing question and nothing is followed. ⚠ The rule is silent whenever the enclosing operation block mentions KeyInfo at all, because there is a correct shape that ends in this call: read signed.KeyInfo, check the certificate in it against a trust store, and only then call CheckSignature() — by that point the key has been established and the call is sound. The guard is per-block rather than per-object on purpose; proving that two expressions name the same SignedXml is alias analysis, and at error severity the conservative direction is the one that misses. ⚠ Two neighbouring overloads are deliberately outside the rule rather than forgotten. CheckSignatureReturningKey(out …) verifies against the embedded key and then hands it to the caller to judge, so whether it is a bug is a question about the next statement. CheckSignature(certificate, verifySignatureOnly: true) takes a caller-supplied certificate, and whether skipping chain validation is wrong depends on where that certificate came from. Reporting either would be guessing. ⚠ Known gap, stated rather than hidden: System.Security.Cryptography.Xml is a NuGet package and not part of the shared framework, so in a compilation that does not reference it the type lookup returns null and the rule never runs — which is correct, and also means the shape occurs zero times in either reference tree.
